trickyParts: The harness is on the issue volume at /legion/harness and is meant to be inherited rather than rebuilt: setup.sh is idempotent (PostgreSQL 17.11 with pgvector unpacked from Debian packages without root, nats-server 2.10.22, the cluster initdb'd as UTF8 with an ICU en-US collation because this image's default is SQL_ASCII with C collation and two existing tests read the difference), env.sh is sourced and never re-derived, e2e.sh runs Dispatch's browser suite on a lane of the role's own. Every cache (GOCACHE, GOMODCACHE, GOTMPDIR, TMPDIR, PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH) is on /legion: a Go cache under $HOME evicts the pod. The api suite takes about 1000 s and the docs suite about 780 s, past go test's ten-minute package default, so both need -timeout 1800s or a bare run panics at 600 s and reads as a failure.

This pod has no Docker, so internal/dispatch/delivery's own tests (and four outbox rows) cannot run here: they start NATS containers. They are CI's, and the multiprocess test exercises the same delivery code against the real local nats-server.

The riskiest part of the change is the document cursor: a missed advance leaves a room permanently behind the head, refused, failed, reloaded and refused again. Every advance goes through one funnel, and two sites the plan did not name turned out to matter - a committed write's versions must enter the room's cursor while the commit still holds the document's advisory lock (a browser append queued on that lock takes it the instant the commit drops it), and a room must record the head its load read plus every version this process appended during the load, because ygo reports a loading room as absent.

A cold write (one whose fork came from the store, with no room) is deliberately outside the gate: its update commutes with whatever landed since its read, and gating it broke TestABrowserOpeningADocumentMidColdWriteKeepsBothEdits, a case the code already handled.
deviations: Round 3 changed three existing lease tests because the behaviour they pinned changed, not because they failed: TestTwoSweepRunnersRunThePassOnceAndSkipOnce (api), TestTwoReconciliationRunnersRunTheTickOnceAndSkipOnce (docs) and TestARunningSweepWhoseLeaseIsHeldElsewhereListsNothing (redeliver) each stopped a runner while its pass was still blocked on a table lock and then read a 'leased pass ran' line, which a pass cut short no longer writes. The first two now count getting into the pass - ran or cut short - which is the property each row is about and which the shutdown change does not touch; the third's stand-in holder takes its lease on a context of its own, since it stands for another process rather than for one shutting down. Nothing was loosened: each row still refuses two passes, and the one that counts GitHub calls still refuses any.

Round 2, after the tester's failure: the plan's section 1 said the design would add no new table. It now adds one, duty_passes (migration 0115), because the architect decided the property stays once per period and the mechanism changes: a lease that is taken and given back excludes concurrent passes alone, and two processes' tickers are out of phase, so each ran the whole pass. The record is what makes a pass another process already made count, and the elapsed-time comparison is made in the database because two processes' wall clocks differ. Leadership was the alternative and was not taken: it brings a hand-over to design and drive, where this costs one period when a holder dies.

The plan's section 9.1 allowed the proof to be a CI run id, since no Docker and no Postgres existed in this pod. That fallback was not needed: the harness above was built instead, so every row of the proof is a local run of two real processes, and the reader-facing half is a real browser.

The plan put the migrations README inside internal/dispatch/store/migrations/. It is at internal/dispatch/store/README.md instead, because pgmigrate.Load refuses a migration set holding a file that is not <version>_<name>.{up,down,census}.sql, so a README there would refuse every boot. The file says so in its first paragraph.

The multiprocess test takes its NATS from DISPATCH_TEST_NATS_URL when that is set and from testnats.Start (a container) otherwise, so it runs both in this pod and in CI. storetest's own DISPATCH_TEST_DATABASE_URL is the precedent.

Three of the six leased loops are asserted by the two-process test; document-compaction (24 h ticker), architecture-import and delivery-reconcile (first pass jittered over five minutes, each process drawing its own) are logged by name with their reason rather than held to a count, because no setting shrinks a maintenance interval and asserting on a jittered overlap would be a flake.

The ce-simplify-code pass applied nine findings and skipped four test-rig dedupes (one storetest lease-pool helper, a Count on storetest.LockedLog, a dutytest hold rig, the second API test handler) as churn across six packages for no behaviour change; they are the pull request's one Fast-follow line.

Three SSE tests of the api package were rewritten rather than kept: their premise was a fake late-committing id published straight into the broker, which cannot happen once the live stream is re-sourced from the log and the commit-order lock is what orders it. They were replaced by tests of the new contract (no backlog to a cold connection, no event at or below a connection's since, a capped catch-up delivering a mid-paging commit exactly once), not deleted for failing.
openQuestions: Whether the new dispatch-multiprocess job is in the repository's required-checks set the way dispatch-memory is: branch protection is not readable with this role's token, so the architect or an operator must confirm it. Until it is, a red two-process run does not block a merge.

Cross-process live co-editing of one document (two live rooms with text streaming between them) is explicitly out of scope here and wants an issue of its own; the documents say so without naming a key.

The preconditions INFRA-63 needs beyond this merge: DISPATCH_SIGNING_KEY set to one value for every replica; the Dispatch NATS user's grant unchanged is sufficient, since this change adds no subject, durable, consumer or bucket (the grant lives outside this repository and was not read here); a deploy check that reads /healthz's commit field will see two builds behind one address during a roll, and /healthz is deliberately unchanged because a non-leader is not unhealthy; asset-chunk and API skew between two live builds is the deployment's, not this issue's; and the front door's stickiness is an assumption carried from INFRA-62, not a dependency - nothing here needs a reader to stay on one process.
discoveredComplexity: Round 3's finding is a written-down wrong invariant rather than a line of code. recordPassOn's comment said 'a pass cut short by shutdown still ran and still served its period' - the behaviour, asserted as the intention - so a reader checking the code against the comment would have stopped there and found them agreeing. The merged behaviour was: the record is written after the pass returns, so a kill or a panic leaves the period unserved and the next tick runs it, and a graceful SIGTERM was the one exception, since the pass's context was cancelled but recordPassOn ran on a context of its own. The fix leaves the period unserved there too, and the comment now says what happens instead and that it said the opposite. The statement of that behaviour reached the architect in a message rather than in this file, because the handoff was already committed when the question was asked: the gap was found after the phase closed, not withheld during it.

Two consequences of that fix, named rather than left to be discovered. A cut-short tick now returns false, and internal/dispatch/delivery/intake.go is the one caller that reads that answer (to decide its bind throttle): harmless at shutdown, since the process is going, and said in a comment at that call site. And a pass that finished microseconds before the cancellation arrived is read as cut short and records nothing, costing one early pass in the next period; that is the safe direction of the two errors and is deliberately not tightened.

Round 3 also corrected two headSha fields in this file that named no commit: 'fe0c2f1c2a6317e1e6e4b0dbc7e0c3f0eca61b0e' (the real head is fe0c2f1c2a631bed1cab81d9548dd49b10c2cf51), which the tester found, and '18438f0b6367a1e2b5c9e8b2a0bbb0d2dd3dba77' (the real head is 18438f0b63673b3aa958c9d6c0c1c911986c00cd), which looking for the first one found. How they were produced: each proof row was written with the short id in hand from the push output and the rest of the hex typed to fill the field rather than read back from 'jj log -r <id> -T commit_id'. Nothing between writing them and the tester's check resolved them - not this file's own shape check, which refuses only an empty field, and not any reader - so forty-hex values pointing at nothing travelled as evidence. The mechanism is the finding, and the second one is its proof: one wrong id is a slip, two of the same shape is a habit. Every headSha here has now been resolved against the repository, which is the check that was missing.

A harness pitfall the next role should not spend an hour on: this pod's nats-server is long-lived, and its ENVOY_NOTIFICATIONS stream keeps a 72-hour duplicate window, so after many local runs TestTheOutboxPublishesEachEventOnceAcrossBothProcesses fails with 'the notification stream holds nothing this row published' - its publishes are suppressed as duplicates rather than stored. It is harness state and not the change: stop the role's nats-server, remove /legion/harness/natsdata and re-run setup.sh. setup.sh now says so at its end.

Three defects were found only by surfaces, not by reading the code. The browser suite went red across five specs because the relay kept a cursor and nothing else, and the suite truncates the database between scenarios, so the ids restart below the cursor and the live stream is silent for ever; the fix reuses the delivery hub's own reset rule (eventCursorCheck) and ends every open subscription. Running the document suite under concurrent writes found the two cursor races above. And the two-process rig built its processes' database URL without the password, so every row passed locally against a trust-authenticated server and failed 28P01 in CI.

The delivery standby has three bind outcomes rather than two, and the third was discovered in CI: on a fresh bus the reconciliation is leased, so exactly one process creates each durable and every other process's subscribe is answered 'consumer not found' until that create lands. That is a wait, not a fault. The same lease is shared by the two intakes of one process, so a throttle that recorded a pass the lease had refused could leave a durable uncreated for a settings poll.
